headline: Lowe’s: the $3.10 EPS ‘beat’ includes 34 cents of tariff refunds — underneath, earnings fell
takeaway: Adjusted EPS of $3.10 looks like a clear beat against the $2.88 consensus, but it includes a $0.34 benefit from tariff refunds. Without it, earnings were about $2.76, below last year’s $3.06. Sales rose 9.3% to $22.8 billion, mostly from acquisitions; comparable sales grew 1.8%.
results: Lowe’s reported total sales of $22.8 billion for the quarter ended October 30, up 9.3% from $20.8 billion. Comparable sales increased 1.8%, the sixth consecutive positive quarter, helped by a 17.4% rise in online sales and growth in sales to professionals and in home services.

Reported diluted EPS was $2.98 and adjusted EPS was $3.10, up 1.3% on the year. Both figures include a positive pre-tax impact of about $250 million from refunds of tariffs paid under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, worth $0.34 per share. The adjusted figure excludes $96 million of amortisation on the two businesses Lowe’s acquired, Foundation Building Materials and Artisan Design Group.

The company operated 1,762 stores at quarter end and paid $701 million in dividends. The gap between total sales growth of 9.3% and comparable growth of 1.8% is the contribution of those acquisitions, which serve professional builders and contractors.
mgmt: Chairman and chief executive Marvin Ellison highlighted the sixth straight quarter of positive comparable sales and credited growth across professional customers, online and home services, which he described as evidence of the resilience of the company’s ‘Total Home’ strategy. He pointed investors to an analyst and investor conference in December for more on growth opportunities.

Lowe’s updated its fiscal 2026 outlook: total sales of about $92.5 billion (previously $92.0 billion), comparable sales up about 0.5% (previously flat), and adjusted operating margin of about 11.5% (previously 11.6%). It expects adjusted EPS of about $12.25 and net interest expense of about $1.5 billion.
The company said the update reflects results so far as well as ‘current demand trends and cost pressures across the business’ — the sales outlook went up while the margin outlook went down.
view: This is a quarter where the headline misleads, and it is worth doing the arithmetic. Adjusted EPS of $3.10 includes 34 cents of tariff refunds — money returned for duties paid in earlier periods, which will not recur. Strip it out and Lowe’s earned about $2.76, against $3.06 a year ago and a consensus of $2.88. On the underlying business, earnings per share fell roughly 10% and missed. The shares rising 1% suggests the market read through the headline and was neither impressed nor alarmed.

Why would earnings fall when sales rose 9%? Because the growth was bought. Lowe’s spent heavily to acquire two distributors serving professional builders, and those businesses bring revenue at lower margins along with the interest on the debt that funded them. The guidance says the same thing in two lines: sales raised by $500 million, operating margin cut by a tenth of a point. More sales, less profit on each dollar. That is the cost of repositioning a do-it-yourself retailer toward the professional trade.

The strategy itself is sound, and it is the same one Home Depot is pursuing. Professionals spend far more than homeowners and spend through the cycle, and Lowe’s has historically been underweight with them — roughly a quarter to 30% of sales against about half at its rival. Closing that gap is the single largest growth opportunity the company has. The question is the price: distribution is a lower-margin, more capital-intensive business than retail, and the benefits arrive over years while the costs arrive now.

The underlying demand picture matches Home Depot’s a day earlier: comparable sales positive but low, a housing market in which few people are moving, and large discretionary projects still deferred. Lowe’s comp of 1.8% against Home Depot’s 2.2% is a normal gap. With full-year comparable growth guided to about 0.5%, this is a business waiting for housing turnover. The December investor day matters more than this report — it is where management has to show what the acquired businesses will earn once integrated.
watch: Earnings excluding tariff refunds, and the margin targets given at the December investor conference. The first shows what the business really earns; the second shows whether the acquisitions are expected to restore the margin they have diluted.
